analysis_sections.body: Prospective, **single-arm, phase I**. Efficacy data for **N=50** as of December 31, 2025; median follow-up **19.9 mo** (95% CI 16.4-23.4). Reassessment every 8 weeks.

Resectable disease went to primary resection plus metastasectomy/local ablation; watch-and-wait considered for primary cCR when the sphincter could not be preserved.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** ETS rate (≥20% target lesion reduction at 8 wks after systemic start). **Secondary:** DCR, DOR, OS, PFS, safety.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **18% (9/50) reached NED**; how many got there via resection, ablation or watch-and-wait is not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No grade 5 TRAEs.** G3/4: lymphopenia 36.7%, neutropenia 26.5%, leukopenia 20.4%. All-grade lymphopenia 95.9%, anemia 91.8%.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data

analysis_sections.label: Applies to

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Median OS 23.2 mo carries a **wide CI (15.1-31.3)** at 19.9 mo median follow-up. Primary endpoint ETS is an 8-week shrinkage measure, not a durable outcome.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: High early shrinkage (**ETS 76.0%, ORR 68.0%**) sits against **short durability** (1-yr PFS 33.4%, 1-yr DOR rate 20%), so durable immune conversion is **not yet shown**. The testable claim, that RT to all disease sites sensitizes MSS tumors to PD-1 blockade, needs a randomised design and biomarker selection, which the authors flag as a priority.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Every pt got HFRT to the primary and HFRT or SBRT to metastases before PD-1, but no dose, fractionation or target volume is reported, so the RT schedule cannot be reproduced. G3/4 lymphopenia 36.7% is worth weighing when multisite RT precedes PD-1 blockade.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The backbone was RAS/BRAF-selected: FOLFOX-bevacizumab for mutant, FOLFIRI-cetuximab for wild-type, each with tislelizumab. Short durability (mPFS 9.3 mo, 1-yr DOR rate 20%) tempers the claim that adding RT and PD-1 overcomes MSS immune resistance, and first-line regimen choice is unchanged.

analysis_sections.label: Results

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: GI G2+ toxicity point estimates were **lower with a rectal spacer in both cohorts** (Gray's test p=0.009). GU toxicity not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: **PARTIQoL** randomised the same proton vs IMRT question in localized prostate cancer and also found no bowel-function advantage for protons. COMPPARE adds a larger multicentre cohort read in the same direction.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents de novo non-metastatic prostate cancer below very high risk treated with protons or IMRT. Does not represent very high-risk or metastatic disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Control event rates came in **far below the powering assumptions**, so the hypothesized absolute differences were never plausible at observed rates. Spacer use by cohort is not reported, so the modality comparison may be confounded by rectal sparing strategy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The null holds across patient-reported and physician-graded GI endpoints, and the spacer stratum suggests GI toxicity tracks rectal sparing more than particle type. It **does not settle** late toxicity or long-term outcomes.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Rectal spacer, not modality, tracked with 2-yr G2+ GI toxicity: 4.4% IMRT and 4.7% proton with spacer vs 7.2% and 8.7% without (Gray's test p=0.009). analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Phase 3, **randomised 2:1, double-blind, placebo-controlled** at 51 US and Puerto Rico centres (26 community, 25 institutional or military). Accrual Feb 2012 to Sept 2021; median follow-up **50.3 mo** (IQR 35.2-63.3).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intermediate or high-risk localised prostate cancer** planned for EBRT, age ≥18, ECOG 0-2. N=745 (496 vs 249); 591 (79%) White, 121 (16%) Black.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Three courses of **intraprostatic aglatimagene** (5 × 10^11 viral particles) plus valacyclovir vs placebo plus valacyclovir. Stratified by risk category and ADT use; ADT optional.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **78 Gy in 2 Gy** fractions, or hypofractionated **60 Gy in 3 Gy** or **70 Gy in 2.5 Gy** fractions. No boost regimen described in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** DFS, time from randomisation to prostate cancer recurrence or death, ITT. Safety in all pts receiving ≥1 injection.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Per the discussant, the DFS gain was driven mainly by 2y post-treatment biopsy pCR; **OS and PCSM not significantly different**.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ TEAEs **8% vs 7%**; most common G3+ event AKI (2% each). SAEs 6% vs 7%, treatment-related SAEs 2% each. **No treatment-related deaths.**

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The discussant set it against established local-intensification strategies: ADT in RTOG 9408, LDR brachy boost in ASCENDE-RT and focal SIB in FLAME. **None was tested head-to-head or in combination** with aglatimagene.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate or high-risk localised prostate cancer receiving 78 Gy or hypofractionated EBRT with optional ADT. Does not represent pts treated with brachytherapy or SIB boost regimens.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Long accrual (Feb 2012 to Sept 2021). Safety population (479 and 232) smaller than randomised arms (496 and 249). **MFS and biochemical recurrence not presented**; funded by Candel Therapeutics and NIH.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A positive blinded phase 3 of an oncolytic-viral agent with RT and **no toxicity penalty**, but the benefit currently rests on biopsy-defined local persistence. Whether that converts to MFS or PCSM, and whether it holds against boost-level dose intensification, is unsettled.

studies.interpretation:
This is a blinded, placebo-controlled phase 3 showing that an intraprostatic agent given alongside curative EBRT improves disease-free survival in intermediate or high-risk localised prostate cancer, and it does so without an obvious toxicity cost: grade 3 or worse TEAEs were 8% vs 7%, and treatment-related SAEs were 2% in each arm. The design choices that matter most for credibility hold up. Placebo injections plus valacyclovir in both arms preserve blinding for a procedure-based intervention, randomisation was stratified by risk group and ADT use, and the primary analysis is intent-to-treat.

The harder question is what DFS HR 0.70 actually represents. The discussant's read is that the effect was driven mainly by 2-year post-treatment biopsies, with persistence or recurrence 19.6% vs 36.4%, while OS and PCSM were not significantly different and PCSM carried a single event per arm. A composite that counts biopsy findings registers a local effect earlier and more often than one built on PSA failure, metastasis, or death. Because the trial is blinded, differential detection between arms is unlikely, so this is not a flaw in the comparison. It does mean the trial has established a local-control effect and not yet a clinical one. MFS and biochemical recurrence, the endpoints a radiation oncologist would weigh most heavily, were not presented in the discussant summary.

Framed against existing ways of reducing local recurrence, the discussant placed the biopsy effect beside RTOG 9408, where adding 4 months of ADT to 66.6 Gy reduced 2-year positive biopsies from 40% to 20%, and beside ASCENDE-RT and FLAME, where brachytherapy boost and focal SIB lowered local failure. Those comparisons span different endpoints, timepoints and eras, so they are directional rather than quantitative. The structural point matters more. The control arm here received 78 Gy or moderate hypofractionation without a boost, and ADT was optional. The trial tells us aglatimagene improves on a standard dose-escalated backbone. It does not tell us whether the agent adds anything once residual intraprostatic disease has been addressed by a boost, or how much of its effect overlaps with what ADT already achieves on the same biopsy endpoint.

Generalisability is reasonable: 51 centres including 26 community sites, and 16% of enrolled men were Black. Accrual ran from 2012 to 2021, and a median follow-up of 50.3 months is short for a disease in which cancer deaths arrive late. One PCSM event per arm means the survival question is unanswered, not answered in the negative. For the trial to be wrong in the sense that matters, biopsy-defined persistence at 2 years would have to fail to translate into fewer metastases, which is possible given that histologic clearance after RT can lag, and not something the current data can settle. Until MFS is reported, the defensible position is that aglatimagene is a well-tolerated local-intensification option with a demonstrated effect on local disease and an undemonstrated one on the outcomes that define long-term benefit, and its place relative to boost strategies remains an open comparison rather than a settled hierarchy.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Local control is the RT read: 2y biopsy persistence/recurrence 19.6% vs 36.4% (p=0.0015) on 78 Gy or hypofractionated EBRT, with OS and PCSM not different. It sits beside ADT, SIB and brachy boost as local intensification, none of which was tested with it here.

open_questions: Does the biopsy-driven DFS gain translate into MFS or PCSM benefit?
Added value over brachytherapy boost or focal SIB dose intensification
Interaction with ADT use and duration

verdict.rationale: Retrospective propensity-weighted registry cohort; residual confounding by indication likely, upper CI bound 0.99 in n=155, and authors frame it as hypothesis generating.
verdict.audience: Advanced NSCLC receiving RT with ICI, newly diagnosed or ICI-refractory

studies.significance: The RT-relevant gap is the exposure itself: the source text neither defines the sequential window nor reports dose, fractionation or target, so the timing signal cannot yet guide SBRT versus palliative-course scheduling around ICI. In refractory disease, continuing ICI after RT gave 11.2 vs 6.7 mo rwOS (P=.20), limited to 90-day survivors.
studies.monday_clinic: In newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC starting ICI with an RT indication, this adds observational support for sequencing RT rather than overlapping it; it does not extend to unresectable locally advanced disease, and in ICI-refractory disease the maintenance signal is non-significant.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Territory-wide **retrospective cohort** from the Hong Kong Hospital Authority CDARS database (**more than 90% population coverage**), NSCLC diagnosed 2010 to 2021. **Overlap weighting** was the primary propensity method, IPTW the sensitivity analysis; RMST was specified where proportional hazards failed.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Of 3522 ICI-treated pts, **335 received RT**: **155 newly diagnosed advanced** and **180 refractory** NSCLC. 247 (73.7%) male, median age 64 (range 34-90).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT dose, fractionation, modality, target site and the interval separating **sequential from concurrent** delivery are **not reported in source text**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** real-world OS after landmark, via weighted Kaplan-Meier and Cox models. Exposures: sequential vs concurrent RT+ICI (newly diagnosed), RT with vs without ICI maintenance (refractory), and receipt of chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Chemotherapy tracked with longer rwOS in newly diagnosed disease but **not in refractory disease**; no chemotherapy effect size in source text. IPTW estimates were similar to the primary analysis.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source notes randomized data on RT+ICI sequencing are limited. **PEMBRO-RT** tested SBRT before pembrolizumab in advanced NSCLC, and **PACIFIC** placed ICI after concurrent chemoRT in unresectable locally advanced disease; **neither randomized timing** as this cohort compares it.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents advanced or ICI-refractory NSCLC receiving RT alongside ICI in a Hong Kong public-system population. Does not represent unresectable locally advanced disease treated with curative chemoRT, or refractory pts who died within 90 days.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Undefined timing window and unreported RT parameters make the exposure **heterogeneous**, possibly mixing consolidative and palliative courses. The 2010 to 2021 window spans shifting first-line ICI practice, and any RMST estimates are not reported in source text.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A **sequential advantage** cuts against the common assumption that overlap maximises RT-ICI interaction, but urgent symptomatic RT given during ICI could explain it equally well. Whether continuing ICI after RT helps refractory disease **remains open**.

studies.interpretation:
The question OCEANUS addresses is timing, and the answer it offers is the less intuitive one. Much of the enthusiasm for pairing RT with checkpoint blockade in metastatic NSCLC rests on the idea that overlap is where the interaction lives: radiation exposes antigen, the checkpoint inhibitor acts on the primed response, so giving them together should do more than giving them apart. A propensity-weighted adjusted HR of 0.68 favouring sequential delivery in newly diagnosed advanced disease runs the other way. That makes the result worth attention, and it also makes it the kind of result most exposed to selection.

The central methodological worry is confounding by indication, and it is not symmetrical. In routine practice, RT delivered during an active ICI course is often RT that could not wait: symptomatic bone or brain disease, cord compression, airway compromise, haemoptysis. Pts in that position carry a worse prognosis for reasons a registry covariate set rarely captures. RT delivered before or after an ICI course is more often elective. Overlap weighting balances what was measured; it cannot balance disease tempo or the clinical urgency that drove the scheduling. An upper confidence bound of 0.99 with P=.045 in 155 pts leaves very little margin, so a modest amount of unmeasured confounding in that direction would move the estimate across the null. The source also does not define sequential or concurrent, and does not report dose, fractionation or target, so the exposure being compared may blend consolidative stereotactic treatment with short palliative courses whose biology and intent differ.

The landmark approach is the right answer to immortal time bias, and the refractory analysis was restricted to pts surviving at least 90 days. That choice guards against the obvious artefact, where pts who live longer simply have more opportunity to receive maintenance, but it also defines a selected group that had already shown something about its disease course. Within it, 11.2 vs 6.7 mo with wide, overlapping intervals and P=.20 is not evidence that continuing ICI after RT helps; it is evidence the question is unanswered. The chemotherapy associations are harder still to read, since no magnitude is given and receipt of chemotherapy is itself a marker of fitness.

Against the randomized literature, OCEANUS sits in a gap rather than in conflict. PEMBRO-RT irradiated a lesion before starting pembrolizumab, a sequenced design, and PACIFIC placed ICI after concurrent chemoRT in unresectable locally advanced disease, a different setting. Neither randomized the timing variable this cohort compares. The practical read is that this cohort does not justify delaying urgently needed palliative RT to avoid ICI overlap, and it does not establish that overlap causes harm. It offers a hypothesis with a plausible biological counterargument and a plausible confounding explanation, which is exactly the situation a trial randomizing RT timing around ICI would resolve. High-coverage territory-wide data is a strength for representativeness within the Hong Kong system and a limit when extrapolating to populations whose ICI access evolved differently across 2010 to 2021.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Timing is the RT variable: sequencing RT around ICI rather than overlapping it tracked with longer rwOS in newly diagnosed advanced disease. Dose, fractionation, target and the sequential window are not reported in source text, so the signal cannot yet separate SBRT from palliative-course scheduling.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In ICI-refractory NSCLC, ICI maintenance after RT gave 11.2 vs 6.7 mo rwOS (P=.20), non-significant and limited to 90-day survivors. Chemotherapy tracked with longer rwOS only in newly diagnosed disease, magnitude not reported in source, so the systemic partner question stays open.

Abstract 539778: Radiotherapy followed by systemic therapy and Tislelizumab in microsatellite-stable rectal cancer
with synchronous unresectable metastases: Updated results of the MIRACLE-2 study
Menglong Zhou, 'Lijun Shen, 2Zezhi Shan, 'Hui Zhang, Wang Yang, 'Yajie Chen, "Yaqi Wang, 'Shujuan Zhou, 'Ruiyan Wu, Juefeng Wan,
2Dakui Luo, "Zilan Ye, 'Weijing He, "Yufei Yang, 'Yikuan Chen, "Changming Zhou, 'Qingguo Li, "Fan Xia, 'Xinxiang Li, 'Zhen Zhang
Department of Radiation Oncology, -Department of Colorectal Surgery, Department of Cancer Prevention, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, Shanghai, PR China
*Clinical Oncology School of Fujian Medical University, Fujian Cancer Hospital (Fujian Branch of Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center), Fuzhou, PR China.
Background
Microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors comprise ~95% of
metastatic colorectal cancer cases and exhibit intrinsic
resistance to immunotherapy. Emerging evidence suggests
systemic therapy may enhance immunotherapy
responsiveness, while radiotherapy could improve efficacy by
overcoming resistance and reducing tumor burden. The
MIRACLE-2 study evaluated the safety and efficacy of
combining radiotherapy with systemic therapy and
Tislelizumab as first-line treatment for unresectable
metastatic MSS rectal cancer (RC).
Methods
MIRACLE-2 was a prospective, single-arm, phase I study.
Inclusion criteria: MSS RC with primary tumor ≤10 cm from
anal verge on MRI and synchronous unresectable
metastases. Patients received hypofractionated radiotherapy
(HFRT) for primary lesions and HFRT or SBRT for metastases,
followed by systemic therapy: FOLFOX-bevacizumab-
Tislelizumab for RAS/BRAF-mutant patients or FOLFIRI-
cetuximab-Tislelizumab for wild-type patients. Reassessment
every 8 weeks. Patients achieving resectable disease
underwent primary tumor resection and
metastasectomy/local ablative therapies for metastases. For
patients unable to preserve anal sphincter, a watch-and-wait
(WW) strategy was considered if clinical complete response
(cCR) of primary tumor was achieved. Otherwise, systemic
therapy continued until progression/intolerable toxicity.
Primary endpoint: ETS rate (≥20% target lesion reduction at 8
weeks post systemic therapy initiation). Secondary endpoints:
disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), overall
survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and safety.
Results
As of December 31, 2025, efficacy data were available for 50 patients (38
males, 76.0%; median age 57 years, range 30-73). Among these, 52.0%
had liver metastases, 8.0% lung metastases, and 40.0% both liver and
lung metastases. RAS/BRAF mutations were detected in 56.0% of
primary tumors. Median treatment courses: eight (range 3-12). Overall,
18% (9/50) attained no evidence of disease (NED). ETS rate: 76.0%;
DCR: 88.0%. Median follow-up: 19.9 months (95% Cl: 16.4-23.4). Among
34 patients with complete/partial response, median DOR: 8.0 months
(95% Cl: 5.2-10.8), with 1-year DOR rate of 20%. Median PFS: 9.3 months
(95% Cl: 7.1-11.5), with 1-year PFS rate of 33.4%. Median OS: 23.2
months (95% Cl: 15.1-31.3), and 1-year OS rate: 93.3%. No grade 5
treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) occurred. All-grade TRAEs:
lymphopenia (95.9%), anemia (91.8%), and leukopenia (69.4%). Grade
3/4 TRAEs: lymphopenia (36.7%), neutropenia (26.5%), and leukopenia
(20.4%).
Conclusions
The combination of radiotherapy, systemic therapy, and Tislelizumab
showed a high ETS rate and manageable safety profile in first-line
unresectable MSS RC. Long-term outcomes require further follow-up.

papers.title: Combination of Radiotherapy and Immunotherapy in Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The optimal sequencing of radiotherapy (RT) combined with immunotherapy (iRT) and the value of chemotherapy remain undefined for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where randomized data are limited.

OBJECTIVE: To compare real-world overall survival (OS) between sequential and concurrent iRT in newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC, assess the effect of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) maintenance after RT in refractory disease, and evaluate the association of chemotherapy with survival.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This is a territory-wide study (OCEANUS) based on the Hong Kong Hospital Authority Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (more than 90% population coverage). Patients with NSCLC diagnosed from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2021, who subsequently received iRT for advanced or refractory disease were included. Overlap weighting was the primary propensity score-weighted method, with inverse probability of treatment weighting used for sensitivity analysis. Data were analyzed from December 2024 to April 2025.

EXPOSURES: Sequential vs concurrent iRT for newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC; RT with vs without ICI maintenance for refractory NSCLC; receipt of chemotherapy.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was real-world OS after landmark, estimated with weighted Kaplan-Meier and Cox models. When proportional hazards were violated (per Schoenfeld residuals), treatment effects were summarized using restricted mean survival time.

RESULTS: Of 3522 patients who received ICIs, 335 received RT, including 155 with newly diagnosed advanced and 180 with refractory NSCLC. Of these, 247 (73.7%) were male, and the median (range) age was 64 (34-90) years. In newly diagnosed NSCLC, patients treated with sequential iRT had significant longer real-world OS than those treated with concurrent iRT (median, 20.3 months [95% CI, 13.3 to not reached] vs 16.0 months [95% CI, 8.3-30.0]; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.47-0.99; P = .045). Chemotherapy was also associated with longer survival in patients with newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC. In refractory NSCLC, RT with ICI maintenance was associated with a numerically longer median real-world OS (11.2 months [95% CI, 7.9-20.6] vs 6.7 months [95% CI, 4.4-17.4]; P = .20). Addition of chemotherapy was not significant for real-world OS. Inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses produced similar estimates.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study, sequential iRT was associated with longer survival than concurrent iRT in patients with newly diagnosed advanced NSCLC, and chemotherapy was associated with longer survival. In patients with refractory NSCLC who survived at least 90 days, RT with ICI maintenance resulted in nonsignificantly longer survival and an unclear association with chemotherapy. These findings are hypothesis generating and support prospective randomized studies to define optimal sequencing of iRT and use of systemic treatment partners.

papers.title: Aglatimagene besadenovec (CAN-2409) with radiotherapy for patients with localised prostate cancer: a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
papers.abstract: Background About 30% of men with localised prostate cancer undergoing radiotherapy with curative intent have disease recurrence associated with progression-related symptoms and substantial toxicity of salvage therapies. Previous studies with aglatimagene besadenovec (CAN-2409, hereafter referred to as aglatimagene) showed synergy with radiation and immune-mediated cytotoxicity in patients with prostate cancer. We aimed to assess whether addition of aglatimagene plus prodrug (valacyclovir) to standard-of-care external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) could improve disease-free survival in this population. Methods We conducted a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial at 51 medical centres (26 community and 25 institutional or military) across the USA and Puerto Rico in patients with intermediate or high-risk prostate cancer. Patients aged at least 18 years who were planning to undergo EBRT and with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of 0-2 were eligible. Patients were randomly assigned (2:1) via central block-randomisation to receive either three courses of intraprostatic aglatimagene (5 × 10 11 viral particles) plus valacyclovir or placebo plus valacyclovir, with randomisation stratified by risk category and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) use. Patients received standard-of-care EBRT (78 Gy in 2 Gy fractions) or hypofractionated EBRT (60 Gy in 3 Gy fractions or 70 Gy in 2·5 Gy fractions) with optional ADT. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival, defined as time-from-randomisation to prostate cancer recurrence or death in the intent-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients). Safety was assessed in all individuals who received at least one injection. The trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01436968, and long-term follow-up is ongoing. Findings Between Feb 21, 2012, and Sept 9, 2021, 745 men (591 [79%] White, 121 [16%] Black) were randomly assigned to receive aglatimagene plus valacyclovir (n=496) or placebo plus valacyclovir (n=249). After a median follow-up of 50·3 months (IQR 35·2-63·3), median disease-free survival was not reached (95% CI 121·78 to not reached) in the aglatimagene plus valacyclovir group versus 86·1 (IQR 29·7-143·0) months in the placebo plus valacyclovir group (hazard ratio 0·70, 95% CI 0·52-0·94; p=0·016). Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) of grade 3 or worse occurred in 40 (8%) of 479 patients in the aglatimagene group and 17 (7%)of 232 patients in the placebo group. The most common TEAE of grade 3 or worse was acute kidney injury in both the aglatimagene group (nine [2%] of 479 patients) and the placebo group (four [2%] of 232 patients). Serious adverse events occurred in 28 (6%) of 479 patients in the aglatimagene group and 17 (7%) of 232 in the placebo group. Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in eight (2%) patients in the aglatimagene group (four acute kidney injury, two pyrexia, and one each influenza-like symptoms and urinary retention) and five (2%) in the placebo group (four acute kidney injury, and one each increased creatinine levels and skin rash; one patient reported two serious adverse events). No treatment-related deaths were reported. Interpretation Aglatimagene plus valacyclovir was associated with longer disease-free survival than placebo plus valacyclovir when added to standard of radiotherapy for the treatment of localised prostate cancer, offering a meaningful benefit without increasing clinically significant toxicity. Funding Candel Therapeutics and US National Institutes of Health.
